books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Stephen A. Douglas, Freeport debate answer (August 27, 1858)

stimulus.source_note: Stephen A. Douglas, answer at the Freeport debate, August 27, 1858 (second Lincoln-Douglas debate). Public domain. Wording verified against the debate text (Britannica, Freeport Doctrine; National Park Service, Lincoln Home).
stimulus.text: It matters not what way the Supreme Court may hereafter decide as to the abstract question whether slavery may or may not go into a Territory under the Constitution, the people have the lawful means to introduce it or exclude it as they please, for the reason that slavery cannot exist a day or an hour anywhere, unless it is supported by local police regulations.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln asked the Freeport question mainly to

options.text: win the Illinois Senate seat that November.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Douglas won the Senate seat; Lincoln’s question did not win it for him.

options.text: defend the Supreme Court’s Dred Scott decision.
options.misconception: Lincoln attacked the Dred Scott decision, he never defended it.
Lincoln attacked the Kansas-Nebraska Act as the source of the trouble, he never praised it.

options.text: make Douglas choose between Court and doctrine.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Douglas won the Senate seat; Lincoln’s question did not win it for him.
rationales.B: Lincoln attacked the Dred Scott decision, he never defended it.
rationales.C: Lincoln attacked the Kansas-Nebraska Act as the source of the trouble, he never praised it.
rationales.D: Lincoln knew Douglas’s answer already, but he wanted it spoken on a national stage, where the South would hear it.
rationales.general:
1. Know what Lincoln knew: Douglas had answered this question a hundred times before.
2. Ask why he asked it again: on a national stage, before newspapers that carried the debates everywhere.
3. See the result: the answer pleased Illinois and enraged the South.
Remember: a question is a weapon when you already know the answer and your rival must say it aloud.
